The core concept of stimulus generalization emerges from the interplay of multiple independent stimulus dimensions, each inducing its own generalization gradient. These gradients coexist in a shared stimulus manifold, forming a complex, potentially nonlinear structure. When physical dimensions such as wavelength and luminance are combined—especially in vision—the resulting perceptual space becomes a high-dimensional manifold where generalization is no longer linear. Neural interactions further complicate this by introducing feedback loops and cross-talk between sensory regions, leading to unpredictable generalization outcomes. The mathematical framework must therefore model both the additive structure of independent gradients and the multiplicative influence of neural coupling. This leads to a probabilistic kernel-based approach where the generalization effect is expressed as a convolution over stimulus manifolds, incorporating both spatial and temporal dependencies. The failure mode arises when these manifolds collapse or become degenerate due to strong correlations or insufficient data, rendering prediction unreliable.
